script_edit:
What just happened? 
An alleged Chinese spy, Jensen Huang, and a massive AI chip project. But there’s a much bigger story hiding underneath.

Jensen Huang acknowledged an affair. After reports described the woman as a suspected Chinese intelligence operative, the chip company’s board opened an independent investigation. But nobody has proved she was a spy, Huang knew, or technology changed hands. China rejected the claim, and the shareholder lawsuit remains unproven.

Why does this matter? AI needs chip design, fabrication, memory, packaging, servers, power, cooling and data centers. One bottleneck decides who gets compute, how fast, and at what price.

Now look at Terafab: Musk’s proposed project for chip design, memory and logic fabrication, and packaging, targeting one terawatt of compute. But filings warn it could miss schedule or fail.

If it works, Musk-linked AI gets supply. Don’t assume prices will fall: reserved capacity could squeeze rivals, while added capacity could increase competition.

Governments care because chips support military, cyber and surveillance systems.

Want to understand AI? The free guide and community link are in the description. Follow for more. The spy claim is unproven; the power sits in the factories.
